analysis.one_liner: Lets individuals and businesses opt into a 17% flat tax and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The Flat Tax Act never left committee: it drew no cosponsors, got no hearing or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let any individual or business make a one-time, irrevocable choice to pay a flat tax instead of the regular income tax: 19% for the first two years, then 17%. For individuals, only wages, retirement withdrawals, and unemployment benefits would count as income, and a large standard deduction would replace all itemized deductions and tax credits. Businesses would pay the same rate on profits after subtracting purchases, wages, and retirement contributions. The bill would also repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes, and it would require a two-thirds vote in each chamber for any future bill to raise the flat rate or shrink the deductions.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most. The flat tax base counts only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment benefits, so capital gains, dividends, interest, and rents would be taxed at zero for anyone who elects in. Businesses gain a lower rate and immediate write-offs of all purchases and investment costs. Wealthiest families gain from full repeal of the estate and gift taxes. A smaller group of wage earners with few deductions or credits today would owe somewhat less, helped by the large standard deduction.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large businesses

how_it_helps.text: Anyone electing the flat tax would pay 19% for two years and 17% after, in place of regular income tax rates and the alternative minimum tax [S2][S3].

Individual taxable income would include only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, leaving investment income such as capital gains, dividends, and interest outside the tax entirely [S3].
Businesses electing in would be taxed on profits after deducting all purchases of property and services, wages, and retirement contributions — a full, immediate write-off of investment costs [S3].
The bill repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for deaths and gifts after 2018 [S2][S3].
Taxpayers electing in would claim a standard deduction ($16,248 for a single filer, $32,496 for joint filers, plus $6,998 per qualifying child) and file on a simpler base [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary wage earners who elect in would give up every deduction and credit — the earned income tax credit, child tax credit, mortgage interest, charitable gifts — and unemployment benefits would be taxed, while investment income escapes tax, shifting the burden toward work. The federal Treasury would lose revenue from the lower rates, the untaxed investment income, and estate tax repeal, reducing funding for public services. Nonprofit and government employers would face a new tax on the value of fringe benefits they provide to employees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wage earners, the Treasury, and nonprofits

drawbacks.text: No credit of any kind would be allowed to flat-tax electors, wiping out the earned income tax credit, child tax credit, and education credits for those who opt in [S3].
The tax base excludes capital gains, dividends, interest, and rents, so the more of a person's income comes from investments rather than work, the closer to zero their tax would be [S3].

The bill would require a two-thirds vote in each chamber for any future Congress to raise the flat rate or reduce the standard or business deductions, entrenching the structure against ordinary majority rule [S2][S3].
Unemployment compensation would be fully taxable under the flat tax [S3].

Employers that are tax-exempt organizations or governments would owe a new tax of 19%, then 17%, on the value of noncash benefits they provide employees — hospitals, universities, and state and local agencies would bear a new cost [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real simplicity and a bigger standard deduction for a narrow group of wage earners with no deductions or credits to lose. But because investment income is untaxed and the estate tax disappears, the savings flow overwhelmingly to high earners and wealthy families, and the lost revenue would have to be made up by other taxpayers or spending cuts — or simply added to deficits. The two-thirds supermajority rule would make correcting any of this far harder than passing the bill was. On balance, the costs to work-based taxpayers and the Treasury outweigh the gains in simplicity.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Burgess introduced the Flat Tax Act on February 7, 2019 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means, and also to the Committee on Rules, the same day [S5].
No further action of any kind appears in the record after the referral; the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing tax code stayed in place: wage earners kept their deductions and credits, investment income kept being taxed, and the estate tax remained. The people better off are ordinary taxpayers who would have been asked to make up revenue if the flat tax and estate tax repeal had passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers who keep current deductions and credits

for.name: Rep. Michael C. Burgess
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 7, 2019; it was his bill alone, with no cosponsors.

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill but never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee at the end of the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew zero cosponsors from either party and never reached a floor vote, so no party split was ever recorded.

industries.note: Electors would pay 17-19% on wages only, with capital gains, dividends, interest, and rents entirely outside the tax base, and the estate tax repealed. The savings concentrate at the top while the revenue foregone falls back on everyone else.

Electing businesses get a lower rate and immediate full deductions for all purchases, wages, and retirement contributions, cutting their effective tax sharply. The revenue loss and the shifted burden onto wage income are the public's side of the trade.
Full repeal of the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes eliminates tax on the largest inheritances. The benefit goes almost exclusively to very wealthy families.

industries.industry: Governments, hospitals, and universities as employers
industries.note: Tax-exempt organizations and federal, state, and local government employers would owe a new 17-19% tax on the value of fringe benefits provided to employees, a fresh cost with no offsetting public benefit written into the bill.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: A simpler wage-based tax with a large standard deduction would reduce demand for paid filing help for electors, though the elective design limits how much of the market would shift.
